title: Puppy Development Stages: What to Expect From 8 Weeks to 6 Months
description: A month-by-month look at what is normal for your puppy from 8 weeks to 6 months, with what to focus on at each age.

quick: From 8 weeks to 6 months, puppies change fast. The socialisation window runs from about 4 to 12 weeks, vaccines are given in the first 4 months, baby teeth fall out from about 12 to 16 weeks, and by about 6 months the adult teeth are in. Every puppy moves at its own pace, so use age as a guide, not a deadline.

faq.q: What is the most important stage in a puppy's development?
faq.a: PDSA says that between about 4 and 12 weeks a puppy has a socialisation period, when the brain learns what is normal and how to cope. Because many puppies come home at around 8 weeks, you have a short window to introduce everyday things gently, so start from day one.

faq.q: At what age do puppies calm down?
faq.a: There is no fixed age, and breed, exercise and routine all play a part. Many owners notice big changes between 4 and 6 months as sleep patterns settle and biting eases, but this is an observation, not a rule. See puppy zoomies for the evening wild spells.

faq.q: When does a puppy become an adult?
faq.a: Puppy teeth are replaced by adult teeth by about 6 months, but puppies are not fully grown or mature at that age, and small and large breeds develop at different speeds. Ask your vet about your puppy's breed and size.

faq.q: Is it normal for my puppy to regress?
faq.a: Yes, setbacks are common, particularly after a change of routine. Our guide to potty training regression explains what to do.

faq.q: How do I socialise a puppy before it has had all its vaccines?
faq.a: PDSA suggests asking your vet when your puppy will be protected, carrying them outside so they can meet people and see new places, using a garden that unvaccinated dogs do not use, and letting them meet fully vaccinated older dogs.

faq.q: How much new stuff should my puppy see each day?
faq.a: PDSA advises not to introduce too many new experiences in one day. Spread them over several days, keep them short and positive, and go home for a rest if your puppy gets tired, stressed or over-excited.

html:
One day your puppy is a tiny, sleepy bundle. A few weeks later it is racing round the garden, chewing everything, and learning your name. People often ask what is normal at each age. The honest answer is that every puppy is different, and breed, size and early life all matter. Use the stages below as a map, and check with your vet if something worries you.

The stages at a glance

AgeWhat is going onYour focus
8 to 12 weeksSocialisation window, first vaccines, short sleep stretches, lots of napsGentle new experiences, toilet routine, crate and sleep routine
12 to 16 weeksBaby teeth start to fall out, vaccines finish, curiosity growsSafe chews, basic cues, keep socialising
4 to 6 monthsAdult teeth coming in, more energy and independenceConsistency, exercise suited to age, manners
About 6 monthsAdult teeth in place, about 42, and a growing teenagerKeep the routine, vet check, ask about next steps

8 to 12 weeks: learning about the world

PDSA says that between 4 and 12 weeks, a puppy has a socialisation period when the brain learns about new things and becomes resilient and flexible. Dogs that are not socialised young tend to be more anxious and unsure, which can lead to behaviour problems and fears. Because most puppies arrive at around 8 weeks, you have just a few weeks to get it right, so start slowly and keep everything positive.

It is also when you set routines. Expect lots of naps, with short sleep stretches through the night and frequent toilet trips, which you can plan using our potty training schedule by age. The first vaccines are usually given around 6 to 8 weeks, with the next round a few weeks later, so see our puppy vaccination schedule and ask your vet how to socialise safely before the course is complete.

12 to 16 weeks: teeth and testing boundaries

According to the American Kennel Club, this is when baby teeth begin to shed and adult teeth come in, and when you may find tiny teeth around your home. Your puppy needs safe chew toys, and the AKC suggests starting to touch the mouth gently so later brushing is easier. The vet may also bring up heartworm prevention at 12 to 16 weeks if that is relevant where you live. Our puppy teething guide covers what to offer.

This is also the age when biting, grabbing and zoomies can feel intense. The tools are the same as before: a predictable day, short training bursts, and lots of rest. Review our first commands and the biting method.

4 to 6 months: the teenager appears

By about six months, the AKC says that all the baby teeth should have fallen out and the adult teeth grown in. If any baby teeth remain, tell your vet. Many owners find that their puppy seems more independent, may test what it learned, and may have a few setbacks. That is common, and it is a good reason to stay consistent with the routine rather than starting over. If accidents start again, read about potty training regression.

How to socialise your puppy at each stage

PDSA's vets give a simple recipe that works at every age. Keep experiences good, using treats, toys and praise, because negative experiences during the socialisation period can make a puppy nervous of the same thing later, or lead to wider fears. If your puppy seems anxious or afraid, take them somewhere they feel calm, then try again later or another day, staying further away until they are comfortable.

  • Aim for variety. Different people, sounds, smells and places.
  • Build up gradually. Start with a quiet row of shops before a busy town centre, and a quiet road before a busy one.
  • Do not pack too much into one day. Spread new things over several days, and keep each one short and positive.
  • Know when to stop. If your puppy is tired, stressed or over-excited, go home and let them rest.

PDSA adds that the benefits of good socialisation stay with your puppy, but you should keep teaching new experiences and keep up training after 12 weeks. Use our puppy socialization checklist for a list, and check your vaccine dates in our vaccination guide before meeting other dogs.

A simple weekly check-in

Once a week, take two minutes to note how your puppy is doing: sleep, appetite, toilet routine, biting, new fears, and anything that has changed. It makes vet visits more useful, and it shows you progress that is easy to miss day by day. If you see a new fear, step back to an easier version and rebuild slowly.

Home alone and growing up

As puppies grow, they can manage longer spells alone, but slowly. PDSA says that four hours is the longest dogs should routinely be left alone, and that this is too long for a very active, young puppy. Build up time apart gradually, using our guide to puppy separation anxiety and our longest-alone guide.

How to use these stages

  • Use age ranges as a guide, not a test your puppy can fail.
  • Write down what changes each week, such as sleep, teething and new fears, so you can tell your vet.
  • Keep experiences short, positive and repeated.
  • Ask your vet about growth and exercise for your breed and size.

Questions to ask your vet at each stage

  • 6 to 8 weeks: Which vaccines does my puppy need, and when is the second visit?
  • 10 to 12 weeks: When will my puppy be protected enough to meet other dogs and walk in public places?
  • 12 to 16 weeks: Should we start parasite prevention such as heartworm medication where I live? Are the baby teeth shedding normally?
  • 16 to 18 weeks: Is it time for the final puppy vaccines, and what boosters come next?
  • About 6 months: Are all the adult teeth in? What exercise and food suit my puppy's breed and size now?

What stays the same at every age

Whatever the month, three things make life easier: a predictable day, rewards for what you want to see, and plenty of rest. Young puppies need a lot of sleep, and a tired puppy tends to bite, bark and get the zoomies. If you are not sure whether something is a phase or a problem, write it down, give it a week or two, and ask your vet if it continues or gets worse. Setbacks do happen, and they are not a sign that you did anything wrong.
